abstracts.abstract: We introduce a novel framework that characterizes quantum complexity classes through the dynamics of entanglement structure, departing fundamentally from traditional syntactical definitions. Our approach establishes a direct correspondence between the growth rate of entanglement complexity in multi-party quantum systems and membership in well-established complexity classes. We prove that QMA(2) can be characterized by polynomially bounded entanglement scaling with specific topological constraints, providing the first natural characterization of a quantum complexity class via physical resource measures. This perspective resolves several apparent anomalies in the treatment of multi-copy quantum proofs and yields unexpected connections to classical complexity theory, including a new characterization of PSPACE through simulation of quantum entanglement dynamics. Our framework suggests that the boundary between quantum and classical complexity may be more nuanced than previously understood, with entanglement serving as a fundamental organizing principle. This work opens new research directions at the intersection of quantum complexity and the foundations of complexity theory, challenging conventional assumptions about the relationships between interactive proofs, randomness, and computational hardness.

We establish significantly improved lower bounds for general algebraic circuits, resolving longstanding open problems in algebraic complexity theory. Our main result shows that any algebraic circuit computing the determinant requires size n^(Omega(log n)), improving upon the previous best bound of n^(Omega(1)) by demonstrating an exponential improvement in the dependence on the logarithm of the input size. We introduce a novel technique called partial derivative space compression that extends the method of partial derivatives to handle circuits with division gates in a unified manner. Additionally, we prove that uniform VP does not contain the permanent under a new uniformity notion that captures natural algebraic computation, establishing a superpolynomial separation between these fundamental classes. These results have immediate implications for the VP versus VNP problem and yield improved lower bounds for several restricted circuit models including depth-three circuits, read-once algebraic branching programs, and partitioned arithmetic circuits. The proof methodology reveals unexpected connections to communication complexity that may be of independent interest, suggesting new directions for lower bound techniques in circuit complexity.

We propose a new computational model called Complexity-Aware Turing Machines (CATMs) that fundamentally reconceptualizes algorithm design by treating both time and space complexity as first-class citizens. Unlike traditional Turing machines with fixed resource constraints, CATMs support dynamic resource reallocation based on problem structure, with state transitions that adaptively manage complexity budgets. We establish that any problem in P admits a CATM representation with O(log n) time complexity using polynomial space, while any problem in PSPACE can be expressed with O(poly(log n)) time using exponential space. A key contribution is our introduction of complexity-preserving reductions that simultaneously maintain both time and space efficiency, yielding a refined complexity hierarchy that transcends traditional classifications. Our model provides a unified framework for expressing algorithmic paradigms including dynamic programming, divide-and-conquer, and parameterized approaches within a theoretically grounded setting. We demonstrate particular applications to parameterized complexity, showing that CATMs naturally capture FPT algorithms while providing novel perspectives on kernelization and fixed-parameter tractability. This work establishes foundations for complexity-aware algorithm design that bridges theoretical complexity and practical computation.

We present a substantially improved algorithm for the Boolean circuit satisfiability problem, achieving a running time of 2^(n/log n) for circuits of size n, which dramatically improves the previous best bound of 2^(n/100). Our algorithm combines new structural insights about circuit topology with refined combinatorial techniques to achieve this exponential speedup. We introduce a circuit decomposition technique that reduces satisfiability to a collection of smaller, independently solvable subproblems while preserving the hardness structure of the original instance. This decomposition approach yields immediate applications to canonical forms of Boolean circuits and provides faster algorithms for circuit equivalence testing. We further demonstrate that our techniques extend to counting variants, yielding improved algorithms for counting satisfying assignments in circuits of various restricted depths. For logarithmic-depth circuits with bounded wire complexity, the algorithm operates in deterministic polynomial time, substantially improving over previous quasi-polynomial requirements. Our work reveals that the boundary between tractable and intractable instances of circuit problems is considerably more nuanced than previously understood, with practical implications for hardware verification, automated theorem proving, and cryptographic analysis.
